en: A Direct Explanation of the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* Composed by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang Explained by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu
Regarding the first five consciousnesses, the verse states that their nature is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they pervade the three moral natures, and they generally take objects of cognition.

There are, in total, three types of objects: first, the objective realm (*tāttvika-viṣaya*); second, the object with a core substance (*sanimitta-viṣaya*); and third, the solitary image (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).

Regarding "objects of a single nature" (*eka-svabhāva-viṣaya*): "nature" (*svabhāva*) here has the sense of "reality. This means that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of form arises from the seeds of the objective aspect;
therefore, it is called "real. This, in turn, is of two kinds: first, those without an external basis (*anālambana*); second, those with an external basis (*sālambana*).
As for those without an external basis, these are the root-body, the receptacle-world, and all seeds, which are the objects of the eighth mind-king (*citta-rāja*). These are merely...

It transforms itself and takes itself as its object, without depending on an external substance (*bāhyārtha*). Nevertheless, with respect to the receptacle world and the *puruṣa-mūla-indriya* (floating-root faculties) of others, since these are transformations of seeds of common-characteristics consciousness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna-bīja*), they may also be said to possess an external substance. Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) directly realizes *tathatā*;

although it does not transform into an objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*), it is also termed an "objective realm" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). Regarding the two cases where there is an original substance: [The text continues: ...that is to say... [the passage ends here].

Now, the objects of the five sensory consciousnesses are the present five sense-objects; furthermore, the objects of the first moment of the clearly manifest mental consciousness, as well as those of the independent mental consciousness within meditative concentration—such as the "meditation-resultant form" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) and so forth—all rely upon the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of the eighth consciousness as their objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*).
Immediately thereafter, they transform into the *nimitta-bhāga* of their own respective consciousnesses to become their objects of cognition. This is just like [the reflection] within a mirror.
Regarding these manifested multitudes of forms: although from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are all like illusions and dreams, utterly devoid of reality;
yet from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are precisely the objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses.
Arising from seeds, they in turn perfume and form seeds. They are not like empty flowers, mirror images, rabbit horns, or tortoise hair; nor are they the same as [non-existent things].

Because the past and future cannot be apprehended, they are termed "objective realms" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). The two realms of "concrete reflection" (*sadravya-anugata*) and "solitary image" (*kevala-chāyā*) will be explained below.

Regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifesting; "perception" (*pramāṇa*) means measuring. When the five sense faculties encounter their respective objects, they manifest clearly;

based upon this, consciousness arises to engage and measure them. Although it lacks the two [types of mental application], namely recollection (*anusmaraṇa*) and conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā*), [it is still direct perception].

There are various types of discrimination (*vikalpa*). However, there is "discrimination by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), which apprehends its own objective sphere without error or delusion;
it is a spontaneous discernment that does not involve names or terminology. Regarding the three natures: they are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

The five consciousnesses can assist the sixth mental consciousness in performing wholesome or unwholesome karma. If they are associated with faith and other [wholesome roots], they are subsumed under the wholesome nature. If...
When associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth, they are subsumed under the nature of evil; when associated with neither, they belong to the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, it is said that they pervade all three natures.
The three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two levels.
The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) pertain to both realms and all five stages (*bhūmi*). Only in the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are the five faculties absent.
Now, to clarify the five consciousnesses: the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue function only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

from the first dhyāna upward, they do not manifest because there is no coarse food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) or mixed odors. The three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body exist only in the desire realm where the five destinies dwell together.
In the two stages—the stage of the earth and the stage of the joy and bliss born of seclusion from the first dhyāna—one can practice.
However, in the second dhyāna, where there is internal purity, joy, and bliss, there are no external forms, sounds, or tangibles to serve as objects of perception;
therefore, the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body do not arise in their active manifestation. This is self-evident for the third dhyāna and above.

The universal, the object-specific, and the eleven wholesome [mental factors], the two intermediate, and the eight great [factors], along with greed, hatred, and delusion—this clarifies that the five consciousnesses correspond only to these thirty-four mental states. The five universal mental factors are:

attention (*manasikāra*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). They are called "universal" because they necessarily correspond to all states of mind. Regarding the object-specific [factors]...

The mental factors of desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are induced by the simultaneous mental consciousness; they are also able to arise with respect to various distinct objects.

The eleven wholesome [factors] are: faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming (*ahiṃsā*).
In the wholesome states of the desire realm, the five sensory consciousnesses can be associated with ten of these wholesome factors.
It is so; however, *prasrabdhi* (pliancy) is excluded. This is because in the first dhyāna, the wholesome eye, ear, and body consciousnesses are accompanied by *prasrabdhi*.
The two intermediate *upakleśas* (secondary afflictions) are *āhrīkya* (lack of shame) and *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread).

The eight great *upakleśas* are *auddhatya* (restlessness), *styāna* (sloth), *āśraddhya* (lack of faith), *kausīdya* (laziness), *pramāda* (heedlessness), *muṣitasmṛtitā* (loss of mindfulness), *vikṣepa* (distraction), and *asaṃprajanya* (lack of clear comprehension). These are necessarily present in an unwholesome mind.
Regarding these ten: within a mind that is obscured and neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), there are necessarily eight factors, including restlessness (*auddhatya*) and so forth.

Thus, among the three root afflictions—greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*)—delusion is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*), which is universally associated with all defiled minds.

The five sensory consciousnesses possess spontaneous greed when they take as their objects the five desirable sense-objects of the desire realm, and spontaneous hatred when they take as their objects the five undesirable sense-objects.
Therefore, when non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings enter the first dhyāna, the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses involve only greed and delusion;
these are not termed "unwholesome," but are instead termed "obscured-neutral. This is also the case for a disciple of the Buddha when entering the first dhyāna.

Because it possesses investigative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), because it is free from attachment through relishing, and because it is devoid of fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), greed (*lobha*), and the eight great derivative afflictions (*mahābhūmika-kleśa*),
it is designated simply as "wholesome" (*kuśala*).

The five consciousnesses rely on the same pure material sense organs (*rūpa-indriya*). These nine conditions [of the six consciousnesses] and the seven or eight [conditions of the manas] are adjacent to one another.
"Pure material sense organs" refers to the five faculties in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). They are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) grasped by the eighth consciousness;

because they can give rise to consciousness, their existence is known through inference. Although they are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they are not produced by the external four great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor are they...
It is visible to the fleshly eye; therefore, it is called the "pure matter faculty" (*rūpaprasāda-indriya*). Based on these five faculties, the five consciousnesses arise.

These faculties are termed the "predominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Furthermore, based on visual consciousness, there must also be the conditions of space, light, the object, attention (*manasikāra*), the basis for discrimination, the basis for defilement and purity, the fundamental basis, and the seed-basis before [it can arise].
Thus, they are able to arise and manifest. Therefore, it is said that visual consciousness arises from nine conditions.
Auditory consciousness, however, excludes the condition of light and requires only eight conditions, because sounds are heard even in the dark.

The three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body further exclude the condition of space and require only seven conditions, because odors, tastes, and tangibles are known only when there is contact.
"Three combined and two separated, observing the world of objects": the three—nose, tongue, and body—perceive their objects through contact;
the two—eye and ear—perceive their objects at a distance. Thus it is said: "three combined and two separated, observing the world of objects.
Here, "observing" refers to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the subjective faculty of cognition; "the world of objects" refers to the objective sphere (*ālambana*).

Regarding their objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*): the five sense faculties lack the function of conceptualization (*ālambana-manasikāra*) when confronting objects. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "It is merely like [an image] in a mirror, without separate analysis.
The *Awakening of Mahāśūnyatā Sūtra* (*Mahābodhi-sūtra*) states: "Its light is perfectly full, such that it is free from aversion and attachment.

However, when the five consciousnesses perceive objects, they possess inherent discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) and spontaneously give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; yet, they still do not possess... [the capacity for sustained conceptualization].
The two types of conceptualization—recollection and deliberation—are not accompanied by verbal designations and do not grasp [objects] as external;
they are still termed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The simultaneous, sudden mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is likewise so.

Only when the subsequent "seeking" mind of the same flow arises does it fall within the scope of the two other means of valid cognition—inference (*anumāna*) and invalid cognition (*abhyūha*). However, this sensory consciousness differs from that, because... [the text ends here].
Only those who uphold the Mahāyāna teachings and investigate with wisdom are able to distinguish them;
for a śrāvaka who is deluded regarding the Dharma, such discrimination is difficult, let alone for ordinary people or non-Buddhists.
Contemplating emptiness through the transformation of appearances occurs only in the state of subsequent attainment; even within the fruition, it still does not fully express the ultimate truth.
When the perfectly luminous [wisdom] first arises, it becomes untainted, and the three types of emanated bodies bring rest to the wheel of suffering.

This clarifies that when the five consciousnesses reach the stage of fruition and are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), they still do not— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

One is able to personally realize the essence-nature of *tathatā* (suchness). However, one contemplates the principle of the two kinds of emptiness by means of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of *tathatā* that arises as a transformation within one's own consciousness;
therefore, this is not subsumed under fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), but is subsumed solely under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Prior to attaining Buddhahood, it remains entirely with outflows (*sāsrava*). Only upon reaching the stage after the Vajra Path does the matured consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) become empty and transform into the Great [Mirror-like Wisdom].
The *āmalavijñāna* associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is called the "initial manifestation of perfect luminosity.

At that time, because the five sense-faculties sustained by the *āmalavijñāna* become untainted (*anāsrava*), the five consciousnesses arising in dependence upon those faculties also become untainted;
this is called the mental complex associated with the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). It is able to [pervade] throughout the future...
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they manifest the inconceivable transformations of the three wheels to deliver all sentient beings from the wheel of birth, death,
and suffering. This is the verse on the sixth consciousness.
The three natures, the three means of valid cognition, and the three objects are mutually pervasive; when the wheel of the three realms turns, they are easily understood.

The three natures are the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. The three means of valid cognition refer to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*).

If this consciousness arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, it takes the present object as its immediate condition (*sahaja-ālambana*) without being accompanied by names and phrases, and does not grasp [it as a self].
Externally, it belongs to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and takes the objects of that absorption as its focus, it also belongs to direct perception.

If one enters the wisdom of the contemplation of the two emptinesses, or if fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*), or if subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) contemplates emptiness through transformed appearances, these are all likewise direct perception.
If one relies upon various conditions to contemplate an object such that the view is neither inverted nor erroneous—just as when seeing...
To know fire by seeing smoke, or to know an ox by seeing its horns, is called inference (*anumāna*).

If one seeks [the truth] erroneously through false conceptualization, one cannot understand according to reality nor harmonize with the facts; such as conceiving a self where there is no self, or deeming the impure to be pure.
It is also like seeing a tree stump and suspecting it to be a person, or seeing a rope and suspecting it to be a snake, or like seeing through the dimness of a cataract.

Flowers in the sky, the visualized double moon, and so forth, are all termed "non-valid cognition" (*apramāṇa*). Regarding the three types of objects—namely, the objective object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), the object with a shared substance (*sābhāsa-savastu-viṣaya*), and the object as a solitary reflection (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*)—the objective object has already been explained previously. As for the object with a shared substance, there are two kinds.

The first is when the mind takes the mind as its object; this is called a "true shared-substance object. This refers to the sixth consciousness, which universally takes all minds and mental factors as its objects.

The seventh consciousness alone takes the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) of the eighth consciousness as its object; this is the first type. Second, when the mind takes form (rūpa) as its object, it is called "resembling a substantial basis" (sādṛśa-sapratigha).
This means that it arises bearing the appearance of that [object], and thus possesses a semblance of a substantial basis, such as when one practices contemplation based on a scripture.
This is because it is not an actual present object perceived by the five sensory consciousnesses. There are also two types of "solitary images" (kevala-pratibimba): the first is the non-existent...

First is the "solitary image without a real object," such as when taking turtle hair and the like as an object. Second is the "solitary image with a real object," such as when performing meditation based on a sutra;
although it appears to rely on that [sutra] as its real object, it is ultimately an image manifested by the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Now, because the sixth consciousness is most clear and sharp, it is able to universally take all three types of objects as its domain while transmigrating through the three realms.
This is the easiest to understand.
Fifty-one mental factors (caitta) are associated [with this consciousness].
This means that, depending on the circumstances, this sixth consciousness—the mind—is associated with all fifty-one mental factors. These are known as the universal...

There are five universal [mental factors], five object-specific ones, eleven wholesome ones, six root afflictions, eight great derivative afflictions, two medium derivative afflictions, ten minor derivative afflictions, and four indeterminate ones.
Depending on what arises, they may be more or fewer; there is no fixed rule for the first group.

Therefore, they must be assigned individually according to the specific occasion, as detailed in the various classifications within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. [The section on] the root afflictions...
The *upakleśas* (secondary afflictions) consist of the six beginning with greed, hatred, and delusion, augmented by pride, doubt, and false view.

The ten minor *anuvartakas* (concomitants) are anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, guile, harmfulness, and arrogance. The four *aniyata* (indeterminate) factors are regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra.
The nature, realm, and feeling of this sixth consciousness-mind constantly shift and change;
its faculties and afflictions, such as faith and so forth, are all interconnected. At times, when it is connected with faith and the like, it is of a wholesome nature;
at times, when it is connected with the faculties and secondary afflictions, it is of an unwholesome nature; and at times, it is not connected with either the wholesome or the unwholesome.

However, when associated with the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayaviniyata*) mental factors, it becomes indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus, the three natures are constantly shifting.
Sometimes it takes the desire realm as its object, sometimes the form realm, and sometimes the formless realm; thus, the three realms are constantly shifting.
At times there is the sensation of joy (*saumanasya*), at times the sensation of pleasure (*sukha*), at times the sensation of grief (*daurmanasya*), and at times...
Painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*), or at times neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, is called neutral sensation (*upekṣā vedanā*). Thus, the five sensations are constantly shifting and changing.
"Movement of the body and initiation of speech depend solely on this [sixth consciousness] as the most supreme; it is that which leads and fulfills, capable of summoning the power of karma.
This means that both bodily and vocal karma are only able to be moved and initiated by this sixth consciousness. It is due to the sixth consciousness [that they arise].
Associated with the afflictions that initiate karma (*karmārambhaka-kleśa*), it can produce wholesome and unwholesome projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
Although this karma has ceased, the seeds perfumed by it can, upon reaching maturity, attract the general retribution (*vipāka-phala*) of the six destinies.

Because the sixth consciousness is associated with the afflictions that moisten rebirth (*janmārdrīkaraṇa-kleśa*), it can produce wholesome and unwholesome completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*). Although this karma has ceased, the seeds perfumed by it, upon reaching maturity...
The state [of the eighth consciousness] is capable of attracting the distinct retributions of the six realms of existence. The collective name for what it attracts is "True Maturation" (*vipāka*);

the specific names for what it attracts are "Born of Maturation" (*vipākaja*). Whether collectively or specifically, the myriad forms of suffering and pleasure are all induced by the karma created by the sixth consciousness.

"Arising in the Stage of Joy, the Initial Resolve": this refers to the mental complex associated with the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderfully discerning wisdom) at the moment it first arises; it occurs when the Bodhisattva is on the initial Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This is because, during the stages of the Requisites (*saṃbhāra*) and Preparatory Application (*prayoga*), one employs contaminated (*sāsrava*) practices.

Through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one gradually suppresses the active manifestations of the dual grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). Furthermore, this assists the seeds of untainted black gnosis (*anāsrava-jñāna*), causing them to gradually ripen.

Consequently, upon reaching the first stage, the Joyous Ground (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one suddenly severs the seeds of the dual grasping at self and phenomena that are characterized by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
One thereby attains the correspondence with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). However, as for the innate (*sahaja*) grasping at self and phenomena—
As long as the active manifestation of grasping, its entanglements, and its latent seeds have not yet been severed,
one must still rely on the power of repeated cultivation to suppress and eliminate them.
On the stage of Far-reaching (Dūraṃgamā), one is purely free from outflows; With observation perfect and luminous, one illuminates the great trichiliocosm.
This clarifies that after the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva, innate grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is forever suppressed.

Although there remains innate, subtle grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), it may occasionally manifest, yet it is not tainted by outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, one is able to observe all phenomena with perfection.
It is luminous and pure, universally illuminating the conditions and capacities of the great trichiliocosm, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate to transform and deliver beings.
Verse on the Seventh Consciousness:
The "Bearing-Substance" [consciousness] is obscured; it pervades both the phenomenal and the fundamental. Following conditions, it clings to a self; its mode of cognition is erroneous.
This clarifies that the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its substantial essence;

thus, it is truly "with-substance" (*sadravya*). Although this consciousness is neither wholesome nor unwholesome by nature but is merely neutral (*avyākṛta*), it is termed "obscured" (*nivṛta*) because innate self-grasping conceals the ultimate truth.
It is for this reason that sentient beings in the three realms undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain.
Realizing nirvana, [the afflictions] universally take this grasping as their basis; therefore, it is called the "universal basis of the mental states" (*sāmānyakleśa-mūla*).

Wherever they arise, they necessarily take the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as their object and falsely grasp it as a self; therefore, it is called "non-valid cognition" (*anumāna*).

The eight universal [mental factors], the five object-specific ones, wisdom (*mati*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*) accompany [the seventh consciousness].
This clarifies the mental factors associated with the seventh consciousness. There are eight great universals (*mahābhūmika*) and five universal [factors] (*sarvatraga*).

The object-specific [mental factors] consist solely of discernment (*prajñā*). The fundamental [afflictions] are self-grasping, self-delusion, self-view, and self-pride. It is only with these eighteen that [the afflicted mind] is always associated.
Constantly and critically deliberating upon the aspect of a self, it follows sentient beings day and night, perpetually shrouding them in confusion.
The four afflictions and the eight major mental factors arise in association. The sixth consciousness is called the basis for both defilement and purity;
the eighth is constant but not discerning; the sixth is discerning but not constant; and the first five are neither discerning nor constant.
Only this seventh manas, in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*), constantly and discerningly cogitates. It is not the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
This falsely grasped characteristic of a self has pursued me since beginningless time, never abandoning me for even a moment;
this is why sentient beings remain deluded day and night, unable to extricate themselves. The four afflictions are: attachment to self, ignorance regarding self, view of self, and pride of self.
The eight major hindrances are: restlessness, torpor, and so forth. Through the six preceding consciousnesses, one cultivates various virtues such as generosity and ethical discipline.
During its operation, this seventh consciousness clings to a self at every moment, causing the wholesome practices cultivated by it to be unable to transcend conceptual signs;

therefore, it is called the "defiled support" (*kliṣṭāśraya*). If this consciousness transforms into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), then all the various practices cultivated by the preceding six consciousnesses become untainted (*anāsrava*);
thus, it is called the "pure support" (*viśuddhāśraya*). For this reason, the first six evolving consciousnesses call upon this seventh.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the basis for both defilement and purity.
"The nature of equality in the initial stage of Extreme Joy— I constantly suppress its effortless activity.

This refers to the seventh *manas* consciousness, which has, since beginningless time, falsely clung to a self and phenomena as its direct mode of operation. When Bodhisattvas first attain the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), [they suppress it].

On the sixth stage (*bhūmi*), the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā-darśana*), whereby it exhausts the seeds of the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpa-grāha*) and also suppresses the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*). At this point, the seventh consciousness for the first time becomes associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
Nevertheless, because the innate grasping at a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) has not yet been severed, one continues to grasp at a self after emerging from contemplation.

One enters directly into the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), at which point the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) no longer arises.
When the Tathāgata manifests the Enjoyment Body for others (*para-sambhogakāya*), it is intended for the capacity of Bodhisattvas on the tenth stage;
that is to say, the four wisdoms of enlightenment (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*) are all subsumed within the body of the Tathāgata’s own enjoyment (*sva-sambhogakāya*), yet their functions are each distinct.

They are different. If it is the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) manifested for the sake of Bodhi on the grounds, it is the function of the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna), and its intended recipients are exclusively Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds.
The verse on the eighth consciousness states:
"Its nature is exclusively non-obscured; five [mental factors] are universal; its realms and stages follow those of its objects; it arises through the power of karma.
This means that the eighth consciousness is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous, nor is it obscured; therefore, its nature is exclusively non-obscured.
It is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is associated only with the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*).
Throughout the three realms and nine stages, one is born only as drawn by the牵引業 (projecting karma) of one's past good or evil deeds; one cannot exercise even the slightest independent will.
How, then, can it be clung to as a self?

The two vehicles do not comprehend this due to deluded attachments; for this reason, they are able to engage in disputes with the Master of Treatises regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the eighth consciousness, which is extremely subtle and difficult to understand.

Fearing that the Śrāvakas who follow the Lesser Dharma might falsely grasp it as a self (*ātman*), the Buddha did not explicitly teach it in the various Āgama sūtras; yet the two vehicles remain deluded.

Regarding the Buddha’s intent, those who cling to provisional teachings fail to understand that this consciousness is the master of the collective retribution of sentient beings and the basis for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;

they falsely deny its existence. Therefore, the masters of the Mahāyāna treatises extensively cite the sacred teachings and fully demonstrate correct principles to contend with them, desiring primarily to shatter their false attachments.
Vast and boundless, the Three Piṭakas are inexhaustible; Profound and deep, the seven waves have the objective realm as their wind.
Pervading the perfuming, maintaining the seeds, the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world, It comes after death and precedes birth as the sovereign lord.

This is the eighth consciousness, which possesses the meanings of that which can store (*ālaya*), that which is stored within, and that which is grasped as a self. Therefore, it is vast and boundless.
Its limits cannot be fathomed; it is profound and deep, such that its source or bottom cannot be found.

This consciousness maintains the seeds of all evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), and is therefore called "the capable store" (*ālaya*). It receives the seeds perfumed by the evolving consciousnesses, and is therefore called "the stored-in" (*āśraya*).
It is grasped by the seventh consciousness as a self, and is therefore called "the clung-to store" (*upādāna*). This consciousness is like water; the former...
The seven evolving consciousnesses arise in dependence upon this [storehouse] consciousness, just like waves.
The objective images manifested by this consciousness act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the evolving consciousnesses, just like a violent wind.

Because this consciousness is of a single flavor, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and perpetually continuous, it receives the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses and maintains the seeds of all phenomena.
My son, this consciousness sustains the internal body of sense organs and sustains the external vessel-world. At the stage of death, it is the last to depart;

at the stage of birth, it is the first to arrive and take hold. Although it is not a real self or real dharma, throughout a single lifetime of birth and death, it must serve as the sovereign lord of the collective retribution.
Just before the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), one merely abandons the storehouse;

after the Vajra Path, the ripening consciousness becomes empty, and the Great Perfectly Pure [Wisdom] arises simultaneously. It universally illumines the lands within the dust motes of the ten directions.
This consciousness has various names. One name is the *ālaya-vijñāna*, because it is grasped by the seventh consciousness.

First, for my sake, this [first type] is called the "appropriation that persists until the Immovable Ground" (*acalā-bhūmi*); since the grasping at a self is permanently suppressed before reaching that stage, it is abandoned first.

Second, it is called the "maturation consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*), because it is that which is summoned by wholesome, unwholesome, tainted, and untainted karma when it reaches the time of its ripening;
this name persists until after the Vajra Path, and only upon attaining the fruit of perfect Buddhahood is it finally abandoned. Third—
It is called the "all-seed consciousness" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), as it pervades all stages, including cause and effect, as well as the states of ordinary beings and noble ones.

However, upon attaining Buddhahood, it retains only the perfect, untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds, which continue to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future, no longer receiving further perfuming (*vāsanā*).
This is because all tainted seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) and a portion of the inferior untainted seeds have been permanently eliminated.
Because it is severed from [defilements], it is called the "stainless pure consciousness" (*vimala-viśuddha-vijñāna*).

Because it is constantly associated with the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) that is supremely wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the "Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom" (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

When this consciousness undergoes its single transformation and this wisdom is once aroused, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) becomes brilliantly clear, and the ultimate and conventional truths are perceived as equal; thus it is said that it "universally illuminates the lands and atoms throughout the ten directions."
Thus ends the Direct Explanation of the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses.
